1	Mpox (formerly known as monkeypox) is a disease caused by infection with a virus, known as Monkeypox
     2	virus. This virus is part of the same family as the virus that causes smallpox. People with mpox
     3	often get a rash, along with other symptoms. The rash will go through several stages, including
     4	scabs, before healing. Mpox is not related to chickenpox.
     5	
     6	
     7	 Mpox is a zoonotic disease, meaning it can be spread between animals and people. It is endemic, or
     8	found regularly, in parts of Central and West Africa. The virus that causes mpox has been found in
     9	small rodents, monkeys, and other mammals that live in these areas.
    10	
    11	
    12	 Discovery and History
    13	 The virus that causes mpox was discovered in 1958, when two outbreaks of a pox-like disease
    14	occurred in colonies of monkeys kept for research. Despite being named “monkeypox” originally, the
    15	source of the disease remains unknown. Scientists suspect African rodents and non-human primates
    16	(like monkeys) might harbor the virus and infect people.
    17	
    18	
    19	 The first human case of mpox was recorded in 1970, in what is now the Democratic Republic of the
    20	Congo. In 2022, mpox spread around the world. Before that, cases of mpox in other places were rare
    21	and usually linked to travel or to animals being imported from regions where mpox is endemic.
    22	
    23	
    24	 The World Health Organization renamed the disease in 2022 to follow modern guidelines for naming
    25	illnesses. Those guidelines recommend that disease names should avoid offending cultural, social,
    26	national, regional, professional or ethnic groups and minimize unnecessary negative effects on
    27	trade, travel, tourism or animal welfare. The virus that causes it still has its historic name,
    28	however.
    29	
    30	
    31	 Virus Types
    32	 Map of countries known to be endemic for clade I & 2 Mpox
    33	 View Larger
    34	 There are two types of the virus that causes mpox: clade I and clade II.
    35	
    36	
    37	 Clade I is responsible for the current rise of cases in Central and Eastern Africa. Historically,
    38	clade I caused higher numbers of severe illnesses than clade II, with up to 10% of people dying from
    39	it. Recent outbreaks have seen much lower death rates of about 1-3.3%.
    40	 Clade II is the type that caused the global outbreak that began in 2022. Infections from clade II
    41	mpox are generally less severe. More than 99.9% of people survive. Clade II is endemic to West
    42	Africa.
    43	 Both types of the virus can spread through:
    44	
    45	
    46	 Close contact (including intimate contact) with a person with mpox
    47	 Direct contact with contaminated materials
    48	 Direct contact with infected animals

    55	 Children younger than 1
    56	 People with a history of eczema

    59	 There are several ways you can protect yourself and others from mpox:
    60	
    61	
    62	 Getting vaccinated. Check with your healthcare provider to find out if the mpox vaccine is

    65	 Avoiding contact with materials that a person with mpox has used, including sharing eating utensils

    67	 If you do get mpox, isolate at home, and cover lesions and wear a mask if you must be around

## What is monkeypox?

According to `doc.txt`, "Mpox (formerly known as monkeypox) is a disease caused by infection with a virus, known as Monkeypox virus. This virus is part of the same family as the virus that causes smallpox." It is "a zoonotic disease, meaning it can be spread between animals and people," and "Mpox is not related to chickenpox."

## Is it currently spreading?

The document states that "In 2022, mpox spread around the world," and that "Clade I is responsible for the current rise of cases in Central and Eastern Africa." The disease is also "endemic, or found regularly, in parts of Central and West Africa."

## Direct effects

"People with mpox often get a rash, along with other symptoms. The rash will go through several stages, including scabs, before healing."

## How dangerous is it?

The document says: "Although cases of mpox are not life-threatening, some people may be more likely to get severely ill, including" people "with severely weakened immune systems," "Children younger than 1," "People with a history of eczema," and "People who are pregnant."

By virus type:
- "Clade I ... Historically, clade I caused higher numbers of severe illnesses than clade II, with up to 10% of people dying from it. Recent outbreaks have seen much lower death rates of about 1-3.3%."
- "Infections from clade II mpox are generally less severe. More than 99.9% of people survive."

## Ways to prevent it

The document lists several ways "to protect yourself and others from mpox":
- "Getting vaccinated. Check with your healthcare provider to find out if the mpox vaccine is recommended for you."
- "Avoiding close, skin-to-skin contact with people who have a rash that looks like mpox."
- "Avoiding contact with materials that a person with mpox has used, including sharing eating utensils and cups, and handling their bedding or clothing."
- "If you do get mpox, isolate at home, and cover lesions and wear a mask if you must be around others."
- "If you are in an area of Western or Central Africa where mpox occurs regularly, avoid contact with live or dead wild animals."

The document also notes that both types of the virus "can spread through: Close contact (including intimate contact) with a person with mpox; Direct contact with contaminated materials; Direct contact with infected animals."

## What is monkeypox?

According to `doc.txt`, "Mpox (formerly known as monkeypox) is a disease caused by infection with a virus, known as Monkeypox" (doc.txt) and "This virus is part of the same family as the virus that causes smallpox." (doc.txt) It is "a zoonotic disease, meaning it can be spread between animals and people," (doc.txt) and "Mpox is not related to chickenpox." (doc.txt)

## Is it currently spreading?

The document states that "In 2022, mpox spread around the world." (doc.txt) It also notes that "Clade I is responsible for the current rise of cases in Central and Eastern Africa." (doc.txt) The disease is "found regularly, in parts of Central and West Africa." (doc.txt)

## Direct effects

"People with mpox often get a rash, along with other symptoms." (doc.txt) "The rash will go through several stages, including scabs, before healing." (doc.txt)

## How dangerous is it?

The document says: "Although cases of mpox are not life-threatening, some people may be more likely to get severely ill, including" (doc.txt) people "with severely weakened immune systems," (doc.txt) "Children younger than 1," (doc.txt) "People with a history of eczema," (doc.txt) and "People who are pregnant." (doc.txt)

By virus type:
- "Clade I ... Historically, clade I caused higher numbers of severe illnesses than clade II, with up to 10% of people dying from it." (doc.txt) "Recent outbreaks have seen much lower death rates of about 1-3.3%." (doc.txt)
- "Infections from clade II mpox are generally less severe." (doc.txt) "More than 99.9% of people survive." (doc.txt)

## Ways to prevent it

The document lists several ways "to protect yourself and others from mpox:" (doc.txt)
- "Getting vaccinated. Check with your healthcare provider to find out if the mpox vaccine is recommended for you." (doc.txt)
- "Avoiding close, skin-to-skin contact with people who have a rash that looks like mpox." (doc.txt)
- "Avoiding contact with materials that a person with mpox has used, including sharing eating utensils and cups, and handling their bedding or clothing." (doc.txt)
- "If you do get mpox, isolate at home, and cover lesions and wear a mask if you must be around others." (doc.txt)
- "If you are in an area of Western or Central Africa where mpox occurs regularly, avoid contact with live or dead wild animals." (doc.txt)

The document also notes that "Both types of the virus can spread through:" (doc.txt) "Close contact (including intimate contact) with a person with mpox" (doc.txt), "Direct contact with contaminated materials" (doc.txt), and "Direct contact with infected animals." (doc.txt)
